extension.summary: YouTube TV live channels and on-demand for Kodi (experimental)
extension.description:
Watch the live channel lineup and on-demand catalogue from your own YouTube TV subscription, playing back through InputStream Adaptive with Widevine DRM.
EXPERIMENTAL: Google provides no public API for YouTube TV. This addon speaks the same private InnerTube endpoints as the YouTube TV web player, identifying itself as the WEB_UNPLUGGED client. Sign-in is by importing cookies from a browser already signed in to tv.youtube.com; Google does not permit scripted password login.
Playback depends on the DASH manifest that the player endpoint offers alongside its own SABR streaming URL. The web player itself always takes the SABR path, so the DASH route is documented but lightly travelled -- if Google stops serving it, this addon stops working and there is no fallback short of reimplementing SABR.
Features: * Live channel list and 7-day electronic programme guide * On-demand titles and search * Widevine playback via InputStream Adaptive, up to 1080p where the account allows * Local licence proxy handling YouTube's JSON-wrapped, rotating-key Widevine exchange
Your subscription, your account, your lineup. Nothing is proxied through a third party.
extension.disclaimer: Not affiliated with or endorsed by Google LLC. YouTube and YouTube TV are trademarks of Google LLC. This addon uses private, undocumented endpoints that Google's terms of service do not permit third-party clients to call; use it with your own subscription and accept the risk to your account.

2026.8.31.77 - Say what a shelf's rows actually carry - Family Feud's Season 24 episodes carry no synopsis at all: the field read last build came back empty on every one of the 186, where Rick and Morty's episodes have one. So that show has a title, a network, a rating and "Recorded N months ago", and genuinely nothing else in text. - When a shelf's rows cannot be told apart by their titles, it now logs what its renderers carried, field by field. "The addon does not read the field" and "the service does not send it" looked the same from a log, and they are not the same thing. - Family Feud's episodes do still differ on screen: each has its own thumbnail, which is how YouTube TV's own app tells them apart.
2026.8.31.76 - The episode synopsis was being dropped - Every episode in a season shelf carries a "description" -- Rick and Morty's S9 E10 says "Tom Sawyer, broh." -- and none of it ever reached Kodi. The subtitle reader looks at secondaryText, tertiaryText and descriptionSnippet, and this is none of those. - It is the episode's own plot, so it is shown as the plot, in front of the show's, which is the same sentence on every episode. - And where two rows' subtitles are word for word the same, the synopsis is what tells them apart now: a show that names every episode after itself still describes each one separately. - Checked and not true: a season shelf does not list the same episode more than once. Rick and Morty's Season 9 answers with ten rows and ten distinct episodes; three of them carry no stream because this account cannot play them, and the versions of an episode stay nested inside it.
2026.8.31.75 - Only the part that differs - Season 24's rows say "Game Show Network / TV-PG / Recorded 5 months ago" on all 186 of them, and two thirds of that is identical everywhere. A colliding row now gains only what differs -- "Family Feud -- Recorded 5 months ago" -- rather than the whole line 186 times. - Two rows that say exactly the same thing gain nothing, rather than gaining the same suffix twice.
2026.8.31.74 - Rows whose titles do not tell them apart - Dropping the offer rows cut Family Feud's page from 383 to 173 and its Season 24 from 808 to 186, and left what was underneath: 186 rows all reading "Family Feud". A syndicated show names every episode after itself, with no episode names and no numbers to draw one from. - The guide already had this problem -- two recordings of one show listing as the same word twice -- and the answer is the same: put the thing that differs in the label. There it was the airing time; here it is whatever the tile carries beside its title. - Only rows that actually collide are touched. A season whose episodes are named is untouched, and so is a colliding row with nothing to tell it apart by, which gains no empty suffix. - A shelf's log line now says what each row carries beside its title, so the case where there is nothing to tell them apart by is visible rather than guessed at.
2026.8.31.73 - An episode's offers are not more episodes - Opening Family Feud's Season 23 listed 380 rows reading "Family Feud; Game Show Network / TV-PG / 5d ago; Game Show Network / TV-PG / 2mo ago; Family Feud..." -- each episode followed by its own offers. - Those rows are where an episode says where it can be watched: one per service, each carrying the same video id as the episode above it, and each with the service and the age written in the field a title comes from. So each listed itself as an episode named after its own metadata, and one of them is a thing to buy rather than a thing to play. - They are no longer listed. A season is its episodes.
2026.8.31.72 - Seasons sort by their number even alphabetically - A folder keeps YouTube TV's own label -- "Season 1", "Season 40" -- and sorts on a padded copy of it, "Season 0001" and "Season 0040". So a show with forty seasons stays in order even if a view is switched to alphabetical, where sorting on the text puts Season 10 before Season 2. - Renaming the folder to "Season 01" would have worked around Kodi's sort by changing the service's own words. The sort title does the same job without touching what is shown. - A label with no number in it, like "Extras", sorts as itself.
2026.8.31.71 - Listings keep the order they were built in - Nothing here ever set a sort method, and that does not mean "unsorted": Kodi applies whatever sort was last used for that content type. A show with forty seasons -- The Kitchen has forty -- then reads "Season 1, Season 10, Season 11 ... Season 2, Season 20", a channel's schedule stops being chronological, and Home's rows stop being the order YouTube TV chose. Every listing here is already in an order that means something. - The addon's own order is now asked for first, which is what makes it the default, with alphabetical offered after it for anyone who wants it.
2026.8.31.70 - A show with seasons opens on its seasons - Several seasons and the folders are now the whole listing. The page's own episodes are not listed beside them, because they are the same episodes: Family Feud carried 383 over thirteen seasons that hold 4,192 between them, so a show that opened on 383 rows had buried what was asked for. 2026.8.31.69 - A show's seasons are folders, not one list of 3,822 - Opening Family Feud fetched thirteen seasons and a shelf YouTube TV calls "Extras" and put all of it in one folder: 3,822 items, with the seventy extras at the bottom. YouTube TV names each shelf, and those names are the page's own structure, so several shelves are several folders now. - The newest episodes -- what the page itself carries, and what someone opening a show usually wants -- stay listed above them. A page that defers only one shelf still lists it flat, because one shelf is not a menu. - What is in an "Extras" shelf is not established: no capture has ever fetched one, and on this account one title answered with seventy items and another with none. The shelf now names the first few things it holds in the log, so the next run says what they are rather than how many. - The folder is labelled with YouTube TV's own word for it. Calling it trailers or bonus content would be deciding what it is before knowing.
2026.8.31.68 - One path for n, in Python, with no fallback - The fallback that shelled out to node, deno, bun or quickjs is gone, along with the setting that pointed at one and the flatpak plumbing that went looking for it on the host. About 150 lines, and subprocess and tempfile with them. - It was never the path that worked. The bundled interpreter answers the player's own transform exactly, and the fallback could not run where it was most needed: there is nothing to find on Android or LibreELEC, which is precisely where the failures it was meant to cover happened. Every time it was reached on a real device it reported "no runtime found" and the play failed anyway. - A failure now says what the interpreter did, rather than advising an install that would not have helped. - The "Cold start the proof-of-origin token" switch keeps its old id so a box that has it set keeps its setting; it now only does what its name says.
2026.8.31.67 - The date parse no longer depends on a torn-down module - Named exactly, by the last build's own diagnostic: every one of the player's eight date literals came back "'NoneType' object is not callable", while the same value worked out correctly beside it. - Those dates are the n transform's array indices -- the player hides them as new Date("1969-12-31T17:30:49.000-06:30")/1E3, which is 49 -- and the parse went through a helper that reaches for calendar and email.utils. Kodi blanks a plugin's module globals when the script ends, so after one playback those were gone and every index came out wrong. A wrong index reads a wrong slot, which throws, which the player answers with a constant, which googlevideo refuses with a 403. - The interpreter now reads a date literal with nothing but datetime, imported inside the function itself. Against the exact failure a real device reported, all eight values that had been failing solve correctly. - The bail probe also called nothing and so reported nothing. It calls the helpers now and names the ones that have stopped answering.
2026.8.31.66 - The bail is a torn-down module, not a bad value - The logs say it plainly: in every run the first pair of values solves correctly, and every solve after a playback has opened and closed bails. It was never the input -- all eight values a device got wrong solve correctly elsewhere, against a byte-identical player. - Kodi tears a plugin's modules down when the script ends, and that blanks their globals. What this add-on still holds afterwards -- it keeps a local server for the SABR bridge -- is then full of Nones where its functions were. A blanked global raises inside the interpreter, the interpreter reports it as the script throwing, and the player's own catch answers with a constant. That constant is the bail. - The diagnostic added last build walked into the same thing and said so: "'NoneType' object is not callable". - So a bail now names which module globals went blank and re-imports them before giving up. There is no javascript runtime on Android to fall back to, which is why this mattered there first.
2026.8.31.65 - Dialogs that fit what they have to say - The sign-in code dialog spent two of its three lines on blank lines and the third on "On another device, open:", which pushed the code itself off the bottom -- the one thing it exists to show. Three lines now, all three carrying something, and the url without its scheme. - Kodi's ok box is a fixed size, about four lines. Anything taller now goes to the full-screen text viewer instead of being cut off, which is every long message in the add-on and not only the sign-in one. - The "no Google API project" instructions are shorter and numbered, so they read as the three steps they are.
2026.8.31.64 - The other messages that named the wrong cause - Playing a channel had one sentence for three different things: a channel no longer in the lineup, a channel with no programme listed now, and a programme the guide names no stream for. A stale bookmark was told "nothing is playing right now", which reads as "wait a while" for something that is never coming back. Each says its own thing now, and the third says what it usually means -- the channel is not in your plan. - An empty message no longer shows an empty box. Most dialogs here pass an exception's text straight through and not every exception has any, so a failure could arrive as a blank box with an OK button.
2026.8.31.63 - Say what actually went wrong - "YouTube did not offer a DASH manifest for this stream" was the fallback text shown for every playback failure, and it was true of none of the ones being hit. An n that could not be signed, with no runtime to retry it with, was reported as YouTube having sent the wrong thing -- which sent a real Android failure looking for a DASH path that was never involved. The real reason is shown now; the generic line is kept only for the case it describes. - On a bail, the transform's date-derived array indices are logged. The transform is pure -- no clock, no random -- and every value a real Android box got wrong solves correctly on a desktop against a byte-identical player and program, so the ISO-8601 parses it hides its indices behind are the one thing a platform can disagree about. Two logs from two platforms now answer it outright.
2026.8.31.62 - An nsig answer that was not an answer - Films failed on Android with an empty-bodied HTTP 403 while live channels played. The cause is in the log: the player's n transform returned "BdHv3wGc_iIzKEBs97-_w8_" followed by the whole input on 4 of 6 solves. Every desktop log across the same player returns a proper 14-character value on all of them. - That prefix is the same across runs and across inputs, so it is a constant the transform falls back to when it decides something is wrong, not a result. A url carrying it is answered 403. - Only the input handed straight back was recognised as a bail. A constant and then the input now counts too: a runtime is tried instead, and if that also bails the play stops with a reason rather than a 403. - The bad value was being written to the on-disk cache and read back for the life of the player release, so one bad solve poisoned every play after it. A cached bail is now dropped and solved again.
2026.8.31.61 - Say which platform and which decrypter - Every log this addon has been debugged against says "Platform: Linux x86 64-bit". InputStream Adaptive picks its Widevine decrypter by platform, so a finding made on one says nothing about the other. The session line now names the Kodi build, the OS, the ISA version, and Android outright. - Nothing about Android playback is changed, because nothing about it has been established: there is no Android log to establish it from.
2026.8.31.60 - The guide keeps everything one level down - A guide row had a title, a channel logo and nothing else. The reason is that an airing carries none of it: an epgAiringRenderer has eight keys and not one is a picture, a synopsis, a genre or a rating. Not one of the 989 airings in the last guide has a "thumbnail" key at all. - The info panel beside it has all four, on 989 of the 989. Now read, the guide gains a 2560x1440 still on every airing, a synopsis on 929, genres on 985 and a rating on 738 -- plus a written runtime ("2 hr") and season and episode numbers where the line carries them. - "What is on now" was still a wall of channel logos. It now shows the programme's still and its show's details, the same as a channel's own schedule, and keeps the channel logo as the icon. - A show has no rating or runtime in its header -- Rick and Morty's reads "2013 - Present" and that is all of it. Its episodes carry both: "Adult Swim / TV-14 / 13d ago" and a badge holding "24:03". Read from there. - An episode's "S9 E10 / Field of Dreams" is three fields in one string. Split, so a skin can sort a season and stops printing the numbers twice. - "2013 - Present" and "1994 - 2004" say whether a show is still running, which Kodi has a field for. They were being reported as unreadable. - Remembered titles are refetched once, for the fields above.
2026.8.31.59 - A show's genres were being read and then overwritten - Rick and Morty's page does carry "Animated, Action, Adventure, Comedy", and the last release said so while still showing none. The reason is the shape they arrive in: this client sends a whole About line as one string where the browser sends it as marked-up parts, and only the parts were being read. A line in one string came back looking unlabelled -- which is how the genres line is told apart -- so every line after the genres replaced them, and the last line on the page won. - Now a whole line is read label and all, and only the first unlabelled line is the genres. A second one is reported to the log rather than allowed to overwrite it. - Remembered titles are refetched once, since a title read the old way would have kept the wrong genres for good. - A wide image is offered as landscape as well as a thumb. A show's page carries no portrait image at all -- every image on Rick and Morty's page is 3840x2160 -- so there is no poster to give and a skin's placeholder is what an empty poster slot looks like. - A page with no genres now names what its About did send, even when its cast came through. That check wanted both to be empty, so the one case worth printing was the one case that never printed.
2026.8.31.58 - A programme with no still of its own - The guide showed a channel logo where a programme has no still, while its show's artwork sat in what had just been fetched for it. The still first, then the show's artwork, then the logo. - The empty fields on some shows are the service having nothing, not a field going unread: "Bathroom Makeover" carries only a list of channels and "Paid Programming" carries nothing at all. Titles that do carry genres, like Rick and Morty, show them.
2026.8.31.57 - The guide has details, and a still is not a poster - The guide gave a title and a channel logo and nothing else. A programme names its show, and a show's page is where the synopsis, the cast and the genres are, so a channel's schedule reads them the way every other listing does -- bounded and remembered, so it fills in over a few visits and then costs nothing. - A show looked stretched because its tile is a wide still and was being offered as a poster. A film's tile is 2560x3840 and is one; a show's is not. Only the upright ones go in that slot now.
2026.8.31.56 - Production companies, and studios as several - Shows do carry genres and always did -- Rick and Morty's page says "Animated, Action, Adventure, Comedy" and this reads it. What was missing was the refetch, which .55 fixed. - Films name their production companies, which the log turned up rather than a guess: "Production Companies: Escape Artists, Zhiv, Mace Neufeld Productions". Those are the studio now, ahead of the provider. - And a list of them is a list. "Adult Swim, Cartoon Network, HBO Max" was reaching Kodi as one studio with commas in its name; it is three.
2026.8.31.55 - Why the cast photographs never appeared - They were read in .54 and stayed blank, because nothing refetches a title it already knows about: every title had been remembered by a build that stored names alone, and a stale answer had no way to say so. What is remembered now names the version it was written by, and an older one is thrown away rather than read. - A show's cast is fetched while a listing is being read, not only when the show is opened -- the info panel is read from the listing, and a show was bare in it. Rationed, because it is a second request per title. - A film can defer its cast too: The Bob's Burgers Movie has MOVIE and LEAD CAST where Rogue One carried twenty-two people on the page. Either way it is followed when the page has none of its own.
2026.8.31.54 - Cast photographs, artwork, and what a show carries, the page's own artwork, and "Rated: NBC" - The cast had names and blank silhouettes: the photograph is on the person beside the name and was not being read. It is now. - A title's page carries a 3840x2160 banner its tiles do not. That is the fanart behind it now. - Saturday Night Live read "Rated: NBC", because anything that was not a year was taken for a rating. A rating has to look like one now, and a show's network becomes its studio, which is what it is. - Shows carry their cast behind a tab where films carry it on the page -- Rick and Morty's LEAD CAST is empty until its token is spent, and then holds seven. It is fetched when a show is opened, which is one request, rather than for every title in a listing, which would be two dozen. - A show gives a span where a film gives a year -- "2013 - Present" -- and the year it started is still a year. - A show has no director. That is the service, not this: three show pages carry genres, a network and a synopsis, and no director line at all.
2026.8.31.52 - Every listing of titles asks now, not just some - 60 Minutes came up "Type: video", no plot, no cast. Two things: nothing had fetched its page, and nothing had said it was a show. - So every row of titles goes through one path -- a category's, Home's, the Library's, a search's -- because "which screen was it?" kept being the answer to why nothing showed. Airings and teams are still skipped. - And a show is listed as a show rather than as video.
2026.8.31.51 - The details are actually fetched now - Still empty, and for two reasons. 2026.8.31.50 - The details reach the listing this time - Last build read every field correctly and put them on the one screen nobody opens: a film's own page, which films stopped opening the moment they started playing on selection. The details are kept now when a page is fetched -- which already happens, to find out what a thing is -- and a listing shows what is known about each title. - So a search fills in as it types its results, and anything played or opened is remembered. 2026.8.31.49 - What a film's page says about it, and films nobody bought - On-demand titles carried a year and a rating and nothing else. Their own page carries genres, a real synopsis, the studio, who directed it, and the lead cast with the parts they played -- sixteen of them for Rogue One -- and all of it was already being fetched to find out whether the thing was a film at all. It reaches Kodi now. - A label the About tab uses that this does not know is logged rather than dropped, so nothing goes quietly missing. - Fixes suggestions on a film nobody has bought. The tab that plays is found by what is in it now. - And such a film says so plainly rather than just failing: it is one to buy, and what its page does hold is on the context menu.
2026.8.31.48 - Films from search actually play now - The typing was landing on the wrong screen. Listing a search types its rows -- folder names and a log line -- and opening a row drew the items straight from the search, still called shows. So all of that work never reached the films: no playing them, no menu beside them. - The row you open is typed now, which costs nothing because the listing already remembered it. A film plays on selection and carries "Extras and suggested titles"; a show is still a folder. - Checked on the screen rather than in the reader: a listed film must be playable and carry that menu. Every reader was already right when this broke, which is why nothing caught it.
2026.8.31.47 - The suggestions were a browser's answer - Asked why we do not just ask YouTube TV, and it turned out it will -- but only a browser. Asked by this client, suggest answers with ten plain query strings and no entity suggestions at all, so there is nothing in it naming what a thing is. The call is gone; it cost a request per search and returned nothing. - The remembering is what carries this instead, and it is enough: "john" cost 24 lookups the first time and 3 the second, "blues" none at all.
2026.8.31.46 - Why the suggestions typed nothing - "john" came back with 24 results still needing a page each and not one typed by suggestion, and the call did not fail -- it answered and said nothing this could read. The reader was written from a browser's suggest, so this client's answer is a different shape. When suggestions type nothing, what they did carry is logged.
2026.8.31.45 - A search that needs nothing asks for nothing - The remembering works: "blues" came back fully typed -- 11 films in Top picks -- with no page fetched and nothing asked, where the first time it cost 19. But the suggestions were still being asked for before anything checked whether they were needed, so a search that had every answer already made a request it had no use for. It checks first now.
2026.8.31.44 - Ask YouTube TV what a thing is, in one call - It will just tell you. suggest answers with the kind spelled out beside the browse id -- "The Blues Brothers / Movie", "Air Disasters / Show", "St. Louis Blues / Team" -- in one 20 KB call for a whole query, where the last build fetched nineteen pages to learn the same thing. - So the cheapest answer is taken first: what is already remembered, then the suggestions, then a page for whatever is left. The 19 fetches that typed "blues" should be a handful now. - Suggestions cover the entities matching what was typed, not everything a search returns, so pages still answer for the rest -- and what a page says outranks a suggestion, having come from the title itself.
2026.8.31.43 - Films found by search play again - Search calls a film a show, and sending the params a real search sends changed nothing -- the same rows, the same counts, character for character. It is the answer this client gets, not the question it asks. - So the page one level down is asked instead. It says MOVIE plainly, in the same header that already makes a film play from a category, and the pages are fetched together rather than one after another. - The answers are remembered, because a title does not change what it is and the same searches come back. Nothing playable is asked about, nothing already known is asked again, and at most 24 pages are fetched for one search however many folders it answers with.
2026.8.31.42 - The search call was not the one a real client makes - Every search in every capture sends params beside the query -- seven of them, and not one sends the query alone, which is what this addon sent. Scanning the request bodies of all twenty-three captures, search was the only endpoint whose shape here did not match. - It now sends the query-independent form, copied verbatim from a plain search rather than rebuilt. Whether that is what makes a film come back typed SHOW is not established -- the browser sent two different forms and typed it MOVIE either way -- but the call is right now, and the search log says what came back typed as what.
2026.8.31.41 - Why a film found by search is not a film - Answered, and by neither guess. The renderer is the same one that works everywhere else and it does carry contentType. The value is wrong: this client types The Blues Brothers and Blues Brothers 2000 as SHOW, where a browser types both MOVIE. 2026.8.31.40 - Which renderer a search row is made of - A browser answers "blues" with The Blues Brothers typed MOVIE inside "On now & upcoming"; the same row here comes back with nothing typed at all, which is why a film sits among shows and opens as a folder.
